resources.string: This guide does not replace an exam by a health professional or a mammogram.
Your guide to the breast self-exam
Do it once a month, after your period starts (usually between day 7 and day 10 after your period begins).

The breast self-exam is a check you do yourself by looking at and feeling your breasts, so you know how they normally look and feel and can notice any change early.

It does not replace a medical exam or a mammogram, but it helps you get to know your body and see a professional soon if something changes.

It takes about 5 minutes and you can do it at home: in front of a mirror, in the shower, or lying down.

Do it once a month.

If you still have periods: after your period starts (usually between day 7 and day 10 after it begins). On those days your breasts are less swollen and tender.

If you no longer have periods, are pregnant or are breastfeeding: pick the same day every month, for example the 1st, and stick to it.

You can turn on a reminder in Profile, Reminders.

Pay attention if you notice:

• A lump or a harder area in the breast or armpit.
• Changes in the size or shape of a breast.
• Skin that is dimpled, wrinkled or looks like an orange peel.
• Redness, flaking or warmth in the skin or nipple.
• A nipple that is pulled inward or points in a different direction.
• Fluid coming out of the nipple, especially if it has blood.
• Pain in the same spot that does not go away.

Most of these changes are not cancer, but it is always important to have a health professional check them.

Some factors increase the chance of breast cancer:

• Being older, especially after age 40.
• Having close relatives (mother, sister or daughter) with breast or ovarian cancer.
• Having had breast cancer before.
• Starting your period at an early age or reaching menopause late.
• Never having had children or having your first child after age 30.
• Being overweight after menopause, little physical activity and alcohol use.

Having a risk factor does not mean you will get cancer, and many women who get it had no known risk factors. That is why it is important to check yourself every month.

Myth: If no one in my family had cancer, I cannot get it.
Fact: Most women with breast cancer have no family history.

Myth: Every lump in the breast is cancer.
Fact: Most lumps are not, but all of them should be checked.

Myth: Deodorant or underwire bras cause cancer.
Fact: There is no scientific evidence that they do.

Myth: Only older women get breast cancer.
Fact: It is more common after age 40, but it can appear earlier.

Myth: If I do the self-exam I no longer need to see a doctor.
Fact: The self-exam helps you know your body, but it does not replace a medical exam or a mammogram.

If you noticed any change, seek care even if it does not hurt:

• The nearest health center or health post.
• IGSS, if you are a member or a beneficiary.
• The Liga Nacional contra el Cáncer (INCAN), in Guatemala City.
• Your doctor, gynecologist or a clinic you trust.

Before you go, write down what change you noticed, in which breast and since when. You can also show your Guíame reports.

Breast cancer is a disease in which some cells in the breast grow out of control and form a tumor. It can start in the ducts that carry milk or in the glands that produce it.

It is one of the most common cancers in women. It can also occur in men, although it is rare.

When it is found early, the chances of treatment and recovery are much higher. That is why it is important to know your breasts, do the self-exam every month and see a health professional if you notice any change.

The self-exam does not replace a mammogram or a medical exam.
Stand in front of a mirror with your arms relaxed at your sides. Look at the shape, size and color of your breasts and skin.
Did you notice dimpling, wrinkles, redness or changes in shape?
Clasp your hands behind your head and push your elbows forward. Look for any change in the shape or outline of your breasts.
Did you notice any change in shape or outline?
Press your hands firmly on your hips and lean slightly toward the mirror, bringing your shoulders and elbows forward.
Did you see any dimpling or anything different from usual?
Gently squeeze each nipple between your fingers. Look for any fluid and for a nipple that is pulled inward or points in a different direction.
Did any fluid come out or did you notice changes in the nipple?

Raise your left arm. With the pads of three fingers of your right hand, go over your whole left breast in small circles, using light, medium and firm pressure. Repeat on the other side. You can do this in the shower.
Did you feel any lump, hardening or unusual pain?
Lie on your back with a pillow under your right shoulder and your arm behind your head. Check your whole right breast with the same circles. Repeat on the other side.
Did you feel any lump or an area harder than the rest?
With your arm slightly raised, feel your armpit and the area that goes up toward the collarbone. Look for lumps or swollen lymph nodes on both sides.
Did you feel any lump in the armpit or near the collarbone?
You did not mark any changes this month. Keep checking yourself once a month to get to know your body well.
You marked one or more changes. Don\'t be scared: most are not cancer, but we recommend seeing a health professional to have them checked.
